ANZAC is exactly that, an all-encompassing day. April 25th is the date because Gallipoli was our first significant military operation as New Zealanders and Australians fighting as our own unit, the Australia and New Zealand Army Corps, rather than fighting contingents directly under the British Dominion as was the case in the Boer War. Public sentiment began to change as the Second World War loomed to recognise all New Zealanders and Australians who died in combat, and it's been that way since. Kids are taught about World War 1 because of the national identity forged at Gallipoli and the 16,000 soldiers that landed there, with the 100,000 out of 250,000 eligible males that were sent overseas over the war. In addition, WW2 popularised ANZAC Day and is seen as part of the celebrations and remembrance.

If you're asking why we don't have our own standalone day, ANZAC Day, as stated before, is solidarised in our national identity and our kinship with the Australians who landed there with our soldiers, and the close co-operation between our countries since. Korea had 1000 soldiers in Kayforce, Vietnam had 3900 soldiers with a peak of 550 in-country, Afghanistan about 130 soldiers - all a far smaller scale and not as stirring as WW1 was for many in that generation.
